property_summary: For any call to fallback with arbitrary msg.value, the call must never revert due to the msg.value requirement (which in P requires exactly 10 ether, always revert if not 10, while M requires 0 ether and reverts for non-zero values) — the buggy version M rejects some non-zero values that P incorrectly accepts, but the rule P actually satisfies is that it always succeeds when msg.value == 10 ether; M violates this by reverting for 10 ether.

For any call to the fallback function with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > current pastBlockTime, the reference contract P always succeeds and completes without reverting, while the mutant M reverts because it requires msg.value == 0.
After any successful call to fallback() with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract's fallback always succeeds, while the mutant reverts.

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, P does not decrease its balance (it either succeeds normally or transfers the balance) while M always reverts, which means P's balance after such a call is never strictly less than before the call minus the transferred amount, whereas M's balance always remains unchanged because the call reverts — the concrete observable difference is that a successful call in P increases pastBlockTime, while in M pastBlockTime stays unchanged because the call reverts.

The fallback function always reverts unless msg.value is exactly 10 ether; the mutant allows any non-zero value, so after a successful call with msg.value != 10 ether the contract's balance can increase and become withdrawable, breaking the invariant that a non-reverting fallback must receive exactly 10 ether.

After any successful call to fallback, pastBlockTime must be updated to the current block.timestamp; the bug allows a call with msg.value != 10 ether to succeed but still updates pastBlockTime, so the invariant 'if fallback succeeds, pastBlockTime == block.timestamp' still holds in both versions — to distinguish the difference we assert that if the call succeeds, the received msg.value must be exactly 10 ether (i.e., the contract's balance change equals 10 ether), which the mutant violates.
For any external call to the contract, if the call succeeds, msg.value must be exactly 10 ether; the mutant succeeds with values other than 10 ether.

A successful fallback call must leave the contract's balance unchanged from before the call plus exactly 10 ether; the mutant breaks this because it allows a successful call with any value >0, so the balance increase does not equal 10 ether.
After a non-reverting fallback call, the exact amount deposited must be 10 ether; this holds for P but M allows calls with any msg.value > 0 to succeed without matching the deposit invariant.

C must always require the incoming value to be exactly 10 ether; the mutant accepts any value, so the balance can increase without a 10 ether deposit, breaking the invariant that address(c).balance is always a multiple of 10 ether.
C's fallback must revert unless msg.value equals 10 ether; the mutant allows any value, so a nonzero value other than 10 ether will succeed instead of reverting.

For any admissible input, after a successful fallback call, the stored pastBlockTime is strictly greater than the previous pastBlockTime; the buggy version allows a call to occur in the same block timestamp, leaving pastBlockTime unchanged and violating strict monotonic increase.

For any admissible fallback call, the contract's ETH balance becomes zero if and only if the call's block number is a multiple of 15; the buggy version's relaxed timestamp check allows a second call in the same block timestamp to break this invariant when it occurs at a non-multiple-of-15 block.

For any two admissible fallback calls with the same sender, same block timestamp, and both having block.number % 15 == 0, the contract's ETH balance after the second call must be 0 (drained) if the second call succeeds; the buggy version allows a second call in the same timestamp, which does not drain because a non-multiple-of-15 block prevents the transfer, leaving the balance non-zero.

For any admissible sequence of calls, pastBlockTime always equals block.timestamp of the most recent successful call; the buggy version lets a same-block call succeed without updating pastBlockTime, breaking this equality.

For any admissible fallback call that succeeds, the value of pastBlockTime after the call must strictly exceed its value before the call; the buggy version violates this by allowing a successful call that leaves pastBlockTime unchanged.

After any successful fallback call, pastBlockTime must be strictly greater than its previous value (i.e., block.timestamp > old); the mutant M violates this by allowing calls where block.timestamp <= old, making pastBlockTime non-strictly increasing.

For any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and a strictly increasing block.timestamp, if the block.number is divisible by 15 the correct contract transfers its entire balance to the caller immediately (balance becomes 0), whereas the buggy contract transfers it when block.number is NOT divisible by 15, causing a difference in the contract's balance after the call when block.number % 15 == 0.
After a successful fallback call, the contract's balance resets to zero if and only if the block number is divisible by 15; the buggy version resets it when the block number is NOT divisible by 15.

For any call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and a strictly increasing block.timestamp, the contract's balance after the call is zero if and only if block.number % 15 == 0; the buggy version zeroes the balance when block.number % 15 != 0 instead.

For any successful fallback call with 10 ether and strictly increasing block.timestamp, the contract's balance after the call is zero exactly when block.number % 15 == 0; the buggy version instead zeroes the balance when block.number % 15 != 0.

After a call to fallback with 10 ether and strictly increasing timestamp, the contract's balance after the call is zero if and only if block.number is divisible by 15; the mutant instead zeroes the balance when block.number is not divisible by 15.

The contract's balance must remain unchanged when block.number is divisible by 15, but the buggy version never transfers the balance, causing the balance to remain unchanged for every call, violating the original's rule that balance decreases to zero after such calls.

After a fallback call where msg.value is 10 ether, block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, and block.number mod 15 equals 0, the contract balance must become 0 in the reference, but the buggy version leaves the balance unchanged.

After a call to fallback with 10 ether and a strictly larger timestamp, if the block number is a multiple of 15, the entire contract balance must have been transferred out (balance becomes 0). The mutant never transfers, so when block.number % 15 == 0, the balance stays 10 ether, violating 'balance becomes 0'.

After any admissible fallback call (10 ether, strictly increasing timestamp) where block.number is a multiple of 15, the contract's balance must be zero; the mutant never transfers, so when block.number % 15 == 0 the balance remains non-zero.

For every admissible fallback call (10 ether, strictly increasing timestamp), the contract's balance after the call must equal the balance before the call plus 10 ether if the balance was transferred (block.number % 15 == 0) or plus 10 ether if not subtracted; the mutant never transfers, so when block.number % 15 == 0 the balance is higher than expected.

After any successful fallback call where block.number % 15 == 0, the contract's entire balance must be zero; the bug leaves a non-zero balance by transferring only 1 ether instead of the full balance.

For any admissible input, after a successful fallback call (whether block.number % 15 == 0 or not), if a payout was triggered, the contract's balance must be zero; the mutant transfers only 1 ether instead of the full balance, leaving non-zero balance.

After any sequence of calls to fallback with exactly 10 ether, block.timestamp is always strictly greater than pastBlockTime. The mutant sets pastBlockTime before the check, making the require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) always revert, so pastBlockTime gets stuck at the deployment timestamp and the invariant is broken.

After any number of successful fallback calls, C's pastBlockTime equals block.timestamp of the latest call, ensuring sequential calls require increasing timestamps. The mutant sets pastBlockTime before the check, causing the require to always fail under the same block.timestamp, thus leaving pastBlockTime unchanged and breaking the invariant that pastBlockTime must reflect the last successful call's block.timestamp.
